unit.title: Swift concurrency: settings, handoffs, time and ownership
unit.summary: Choose safe execution and ownership rules, test deadlines and channel demand, and explain who releases native resources.

lessons.title: Moving to Swift 6: check rules and execution settings separately
lessons.summary: Compare compiler checks and actor defaults one setting at a time, then review where CPU work runs before adopting them.
objectives: Record compiler version, language mode, package tools, isolation defaults and OS requirements separately.
Reproduce a warning becoming an error and a change in where an async call executes.
Review UI responsiveness, cancellation and state ownership before changing execution defaults.

sections.title: A new compiler does not change every target's rules
sections.html:
Installing a new tool and choosing new rules are different actions. Swift 6 language mode enforces data-race safety checking, but installing a Swift 6 compiler does not enable that mode in every target. A target is a separately built part of an app or package. Swift 6.2 also introduced settings that change inferred actor isolation and where ordinary nonisolated async functions execute. Those are additional choices. Android teams similarly separate compiler diagnostics from coroutine execution policy. Change these inputs independently so a successful build tells you which rule was actually checked.

Sessions 015 and 016 already establish task ownership, actor reentrancy and Sendable. This lesson adds a repeatable experiment: the same bounded source is compiled under several explicit settings, with an expected diagnostic category. A warning under Swift 5 and an error under Swift 6 are distinct observations. Neither proves a race occurred in a running process. They show which contract the compiler enforces. A settings-only change can also alter where synchronous work executes, so migration review must include responsiveness and cancellation behavior.

Use synthetic names and scratch files. The lab never compiles the company application. Before changing any real module, name its owner, callers, dependent modules, supported compiler and test destinations. A module that publishes general-purpose APIs has different isolation needs from a UI-only executable. There is no universal instruction to mark all declarations MainActor or to convert every warning into an unchecked conformance.

sections.title: Record the settings that affect this build
sections.html:
A compiler version names the tool reading your source. A language mode names the rules it uses for that target. A package tools-version header sets minimum tools and manifest APIs; the manifest is the package's build description. These are separate inputs. swiftc -swift-version 5 or 6 chooses the language mode. This lab requires tools 6.2 and explicitly selects swiftLanguageModes: [.v6]. Default isolation chooses inferred actor ownership, and upcoming feature flags opt into additional language behaviour. Record all five: compiler, language mode, tools version, default isolation and feature flags. You will then know what each result can support.

Runtime and SDK availability remain separate. Recognizing @concurrent with a sufficiently new compiler does not make every framework API in its body available on an older phone. The companion ManualClock uses Synchronization.Mutex and a macOS 15 minimum; that is a host-library requirement, not a claim that the syntax needs iOS 18. The production helper inspected at line 20 supplies SWIFT_VERSION: "6" to selected package targets. It does not establish that all app targets use Swift 6, that default isolation is MainActor, or that the caller-execution feature is enabled.

Android's languageVersion, Gradle plugin, compileSdk and minSdk provide a useful checklist of independent dimensions. Their values do not map numerically to Swift or iOS versions. Read the consuming target's resolved compile command before asserting effective settings. This course inspects declared settings only; generated-client builds and resolved Xcode settings remain unverified.

sections.title: Compile the unsafe counter; do not run it
sections.html:
A shared counter needs a rule saying who may change it. This fixture deliberately has no such owner: counter is mutable module-level storage, and increment performs a read-modify-write. Compile it as a library, so executable top-level code's special MainActor treatment does not hide the intended diagnostic. The recorded Swift 5 mode with complete checking produces a warning and succeeds. Swift 6 mode rejects it. The diagnostic verifier records both the exit status and error category in unique temporary logs and object outputs. This is evidence about checking rules; no unsafe increment is executed.

var counter = 0
func increment() { counter += 1 }
// Compile as a library, never run this diagnostic fixture.
// swiftc -parse-as-library -c -swift-version 5 \
//   -strict-concurrency=complete MutableGlobal.swift -o /private/tmp/global.o
// Repeat with -swift-version 6.

Repair according to actual use. A UI-owned counter can live under MainActor; an account-owned counter can belong to an actor; a constant can become immutable if it truly never changes. Suppressing the warning does not invent synchronization. Swift 5 complete checking lets a team classify and fix boundaries incrementally before enforcing Swift 6 errors. Swift 6 complete checking is enforced regardless of reducing the old strict-concurrency setting. An error budget must therefore track unresolved ownership decisions rather than recommending targeted checking as a Swift 6 escape.

A Java volatile field does not make a compound increment atomic, and a Kotlin val containing a mutable object does not make its internals safe. These familiar mistakes explain why a migration should ask who can mutate the storage, not merely whether its declaration looks immutable.

sections.title: Check one default at a time
sections.html:
Default isolation is the actor-access rule inferred when a declaration does not specify one. SE-0466 defines -default-isolation MainActor and nonisolated. The compiler default remains nonisolated when you make no explicit choice; a project template can opt in to MainActor. Inference applies to that compiled module, with exceptions, and does not rewrite imported libraries. Explicit isolation and actor declarations still matter. So do SendableMetatype rules, which concern type values safe across isolation boundaries. Begin with the small free function below before interpreting a complicated generic type.

func uiValue() -> Int { 1 }
nonisolated func outside() -> Int { uiValue() }

The first function returns an integer without suspension. The second explicitly opts out of actor isolation and calls the first synchronously. With default-isolation nonisolated this compiles. With default-isolation MainActor the first function becomes isolated and the call is rejected. The body is trivial, but the changed API contract is real. Adding await would also require an asynchronous caller and a deliberate cross-actor access design.

InputMeaningCompanion observation
Swift 5, complete checkingStage stricter checkingMutable-global warning
Swift 6Enforce race-safety errorsMutable-global rejection
Default nonisolated / MainActorChoose module inferenceOutside call passes / fails
NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault off / onChoose ordinary nonisolated async executionActor-held worker call fails / passes
@concurrent with feature onExplicitly leave caller actorUnsafe worker call still fails

SwiftPM 6.2 exposes .defaultIsolation(MainActor.self) or .defaultIsolation(nil), plus .enableUpcomingFeature("NonisolatedNonsendingByDefault"). Apply settings to each intended target, including tests. This table describes language/compiler cases verified with Swift 6.4, not an effective-setting audit of any Xcode app.

sections.title: Async work can remain with its caller
sections.html:
Actor isolation controls who may access mutable state; it does not assign an actor a private thread. In this fixture, Owner protects a mutable Worker. Worker.step is async but contains no suspension, so its increment still occupies the executing thread. The caller-execution feature keeps this call in Owner's actor context and the recorded fixture compiles. Without that feature, legacy nonisolated-async execution leaves Owner's executor, allowing other actor work to reach the same Worker concurrently; the fixture is rejected. Follow the reference across that boundary, rather than assuming async itself supplies safety.

final class Worker {
    var count = 0
    nonisolated func step() async { count += 1 }
}
actor Owner {
    let worker = Worker()
    func run() async { await worker.step() }
}

Swift 6.2 offers nonisolated(nonsending) to request caller execution explicitly, and @concurrent to leave the caller's actor. Changing step to @concurrent makes the unsafe cross-domain call fail even with the feature enabled. This annotation changes execution behaviour. It creates no new task, promises no dedicated thread, and makes no mutable reference safe to share. Nor does it split a loop into parallel pieces. A pure computation with Sendable input and output is a better candidate for that boundary.

Kotlin withContext(Dispatchers.Default) is an analogy for deliberately moving expensive work away from a UI dispatcher, but @concurrent specifies Swift actor-execution behavior rather than selecting a named Kotlin dispatcher or thread pool. Caller-isolated parsing can now occupy MainActor until it suspends. A request API that mostly waits for I/O may fit caller execution; large synchronous decoding needs a measured execution policy and safe snapshots. A changed setting can preserve race safety while worsening rendering.

sections.title: Preserve stop requests, errors and recovery
sections.html:
Cancellation asks work to stop. Neither actor isolation nor @concurrent automatically checks that request. A migrated function must still preserve thrown errors, keep CancellationError recognisable, and check for cancellation between useful chunks of CPU work. A legacy request may finish after cancellation was requested. Keep request-generation checks so its old result cannot overwrite a newer one. A generation is an identity that marks which request remains current. Session 016 supplies that earlier ownership practice. This settings lab adds checks for new boundaries; it does not replace cancellation or stale-result tests.

For each diagnostic choose one owner and an API strategy: isolated mutation, immutable snapshot, verified transfer, or a bounded legacy adapter. Review public actor annotations as caller-visible changes. If a module defaults to MainActor, explicitly identify its APIs intended for unrestricted callers; moving a type into that module can change inference without a source annotation. Validate both consuming and producing modules on supported compilers. A green scratch matrix cannot establish binary compatibility, production performance or successful deployment.

A staged rollout first enables complete checking in Swift 5, resolves ownership errors, then enables Swift 6 in a small dependency leaf. Treat default MainActor and caller execution as separately reviewable changes with independent rollback settings. Keep before/after logs, compiler identity and deterministic cancellation tests. For responsiveness, define a target/device recording plan; do not fill its results from host timings. This lesson supplies executable language evidence while leaving organizational approval and real application adoption pending.

quiz.question: A Swift 6.4 compiler builds a target in Swift 5 mode. What follows?
options: Swift 6 race-safety errors are automatically enforced everywhere.
Compiler capability and target language mode are separate.
The target must deploy only to iOS 26.
quiz.explanation: A new compiler can retain Swift 5 compatibility. Complete checking can stage warnings; language mode selects enforcement. Deployment requirements depend on APIs, not the compiler's version number.

quiz.question: With caller execution enabled, why can @concurrent still reject an actor-held mutable worker?
options: It explicitly leaves the caller actor and the reference is not safe to share.
It cancels the owner actor.
It creates an isolated copy of the worker.
quiz.explanation: The explicit execution boundary exposes potential concurrent access. It provides neither copying nor cancellation and does not imply Sendable.

quiz.question: What does default-isolation MainActor change?
options: All imported modules.
Every actor into the same actor.
Eligible unannotated declarations within the compiled module.
quiz.explanation: Default inference is module-local and has documented exceptions. Explicit actor isolation and imported API contracts remain meaningful.

exercise.brief: Record the migration fixture results with their settings. Then propose separate steps for checking rules and UI execution policy.
steps: Run the diagnostic verifier with a Swift 6.2 or newer compiler and keep the unique evidence directory it reports.
Predict each matrix row before opening its log.
Explain two repairs to shared-state ownership. Separately assess what caller-executed synchronous parsing would do to the UI.
Name one rollback for language checking and another for execution defaults.
acceptance: The record names compiler version, language mode, default isolation, feature flags and expected diagnostic categories.
A Swift 5 warning is distinguished from a Swift 6 compilation error.
The feature-on Worker case compiles, while the @concurrent Worker case is rejected.
The report makes no claim that the client migrated or that target responsiveness was measured.
exercise.solution:
A result record must name both the tool and its chosen rules. The earlier author run used Apple Swift 6.4. MutableGlobal.swift warned under Swift 5 with complete checking and was rejected under Swift 6. DefaultIsolation.swift passed with nonisolated inference and failed with MainActor inference. CallerIsolation.swift failed with the feature off and passed with it on. ConcurrentBoundary.swift remained rejected with the feature on. The verifier saves complete logs and object outputs in temporary directories. It compiles the invalid fixtures without executing them; reproduce and record your own results.

For the counter, choose MainActor only if every legitimate mutation belongs to UI state. Otherwise put the state in an actor whose lifetime matches the feature or account. For Worker, caller execution fits only if actor ownership is intended and its synchronous work has an acceptable cost. A general-purpose parser can take Sendable inputs and use @concurrent when deliberately leaving the UI actor. That does not remove the need to measure its responsiveness. A blanket unchecked annotation supplies neither ownership nor safe execution.

Keep three review items separate: Swift 5 complete checking, Swift 6 enforcement, and the newer inference/execution settings. Turning off the caller-execution feature restores legacy nonisolated-async execution. It does not repair the shared-state warning that motivated the language migration. Scratch compilation checks the static contract; a representative target recording checks UI responsiveness. Keep cancellation and stale-result tests from the earlier lessons, then add tests for the changed source boundaries. Supply your own logs and decisions before treating the proposed migration as accepted.

simple.story: A workshop gets a new inspection tool. Installing it does not decide which rulebook every bench uses. One bench still uses the old rules and receives a warning about an unsecured box. Another uses the new rules and must fix the box before work can pass inspection. A separate sign says which work belongs at the front desk. Changing that sign can move work there even when it passes every safety check. The manager records the tool, rulebook and desk sign separately, so a successful inspection does not hide a change in where work happens.
simple.meaning: Compiler version, Swift language mode and default isolation are different inputs. Swift 5 complete checking can warn about shared mutable state; Swift 6 rejects the same fixture. MainActor defaults and caller-execution settings separately affect API isolation and where async work runs.

example.before: MutableGlobal.swift declares an unisolated mutable counter. It is compiled as a library in Swift 5 mode with complete concurrency checking.
example.change: Compile the same source in Swift 6 mode, keeping the diagnostic fixture unexecuted.
example.after: The recorded Swift 5 case succeeds with a concurrency warning; the Swift 6 case fails with an error. No runtime race is demonstrated.

The compatibility and checking rules selected for a target, even when the compiler is newer.
A package's minimum tools and manifest API requirement, separate from its target language mode.
The actor-access rule inferred for declarations that do not state their own rule, subject to exceptions.
Async work remaining in the caller's actor context under the relevant annotation or setting.
A compiler warning or error about source; it is not a recording of a runtime failure.

simple.remember: Write down which setting changed before explaining why a build changed.
simple.boundary: A compiler is not a workplace inspector, and no setting gives actors dedicated threads. Static checking does not prove UI responsiveness, complete cancellation handling, OS availability, or that all production targets use the inspected settings.

lessons.title: Sharing or handing over data: actor and API access rules
lessons.summary: Choose whether data stays safe to share or moves to one owner, then make actor and protocol access rules explicit.
objectives: Explain a one-way transfer and why it does not make a mutable class generally safe to share.
Use an isolated parameter or conformance to name where an API may be used.
Design a small legacy adapter with named owners, errors, stop requests and cleanup.

sections.title: Decide who may keep using the object
sections.html:
If two people keep editing the same draft, calling one reference read-only does not protect the paper. An Android val similarly prevents rebinding without preventing mutation inside the object. Decide whether callers need a separate snapshot, access through one owner, or a complete handoff. Swift's Sendable says values of a type are safe across concurrency domains. sending states a transfer requirement at one parameter or result boundary. Neither creates a deep copy. Choose the ownership meaning first, then the annotation that checks it.

Session 016 already teaches why actors serialize protected state but remain reentrant. The added idea is an isolation region: values and their aliases tracked together for transfer safety. A non-Sendable value can sometimes cross when the compiler can prove that its reachable mutable state is disconnected from state concurrently accessible elsewhere and that the source does not access the region afterward. Two variable names can reach the same object. Giving up one name is insufficient if the source keeps using another alias.

Do not assume that successful transfer makes the type generally safe to share. A Draft handed once to an actor can remain a plain mutable class. The actor controls subsequent mutation and returns immutable snapshots. If the screen still needs its draft, construct a separate value snapshot or copy before transferring, with a defined policy for referenced children. The choice is about API meaning, not making a diagnostic disappear.

sections.title: Hand the draft to one actor
sections.html:
A sending parameter requires a value safe to hand across this isolation boundary. In the example, Draft is a mutable class; final prevents subclasses, not changes to text. Inbox is an actor, which controls access to its stored draft rather than owning a dedicated thread. Its optional draft starts empty. install omits the external label with an underscore and stores the transferred reference. deliver creates a fresh Draft("fixture") and never uses it after installation. snapshot returns only optional String text, so the caller receives a Sendable value instead of the mutable object.

final class Draft {
    var text: String
    init(_ text: String) { self.text = text }
}
actor Inbox {
    private var draft: Draft?
    func install(_ draft: sending Draft) { self.draft = draft }
    func snapshot() -> String? { draft?.text }
}
func deliver(to inbox: Inbox) async -> String? {
    let draft = Draft("fixture")
    await inbox.install(draft)
    return await inbox.snapshot()
}

Snapshot reads the actor-owned object and returns an optional String, a Sendable value. Deliver creates a fresh local instance, awaits installation, then asks only for that snapshot. It never accesses the transferred reference again. These declarations compile standalone in Swift 6 language mode and are represented by the package's DraftInbox check. Diagnostics/Transfer.swift adds an INVALID branch that reads the original payload after sending; the diagnostic verifier confirms rejection without running unsafe code.

Sending also applies to result values, for example a factory returning a fresh disconnected reference. That is still a transfer contract at the return boundary. It does not say the returned class has value semantics. Sending is distinct from consuming, covered in lesson 092: consuming specifies ownership conventions and use of an owned value, while sending specifies isolation-region transfer. Conflating them obscures both aliases and lifetimes.

sections.title: Share a safe snapshot without giving up your copy
sections.html:
Sharing means the original value can remain usable while another concurrency domain receives a value safe for that boundary. A snapshot containing only Sendable value members is a simple example. An array of strings can cross while the original array remains usable; its value semantics preserve the independence of mutations. A reference type can also be Sendable, such as an actor or a carefully designed immutable final class. A mutable class with unprotected state needs an owner or verified synchronisation. Declaring its reference with let still permits changes inside the referenced object.

struct DraftSnapshot: Sendable {
    let text: String
    let revision: Int
}
typealias Loader = @Sendable (String) async throws -> DraftSnapshot

The struct's fields are Sendable values. The typealias names a closure contract, not a class. @Sendable constrains captures and concurrent use of the closure; async permits suspension; throws preserves failure; and the result has an explicit cross-domain shape. A loader can capture an actor reference that owns its mutable cache. It should not capture a mutable test counter without an ownership policy. This declaration snippet requires a Swift concurrency-capable compiler; no networking actually runs.

Kotlin immutable data classes and Java 11 classes with final fields are useful snapshot analogies, with a critical boundary: neither automatically proves deep immutability or Swift-style checked cross-domain access. A Kotlin data class holding MutableList remains mutable through that list. Swift similarly examines stored members and isolation. @unchecked Sendable is a programmer assertion bypassing compiler verification, not a conversion into safe data. If used in a legacy adapter, its documented invariant must cover every access, including teardown and callbacks.

sections.title: Enter one actor for a whole synchronous batch
sections.html:
An isolated parameter says this function runs under the named actor's access rules. Ledger owns total, and its synchronous add changes that total. private(set) restricts the setter but does not replace actor isolation. batch enters one Ledger's domain, adds 2, adds 3 and reads total without await inside its body. An outside caller such as sample awaits entry. Because the batch contains no suspension, another actor job cannot interleave between these updates. The host companion checks the result 5. That result relies on access rules, not thread identity or scheduling order.

actor Ledger {
    private(set) var total = 0
    func add(_ amount: Int) { total += amount }
}
func batch(_ ledger: isolated Ledger) -> Int {
    ledger.add(2)
    ledger.add(3)
    return ledger.total
}
func sample() async -> Int { await batch(Ledger()) }

Because this batch is synchronous, it has no reentrant suspension between its updates. Adding an await inside a redesigned batch would permit interleaving again; isolated is not a transaction lock held across arbitrary asynchronous work. Ordinary isolated actor parameters select one actor domain; they do not provide a convenient way to hold several independent actors simultaneously. Design cross-actor operations around snapshots, reservations and explicit recovery instead.

For caller-selected isolation, modern APIs can accept isolation: isolated (any Actor)? = #isolation. The default captures the caller's isolation where available; the body must still respect type and region rules. This is a language mechanism, unlike Kotlin Receiver syntax, which changes available member names without itself proving actor confinement. Use the small concrete Ledger example first, then study generic isolation only when the API needs it.

sections.title: State where a protocol implementation may be used
sections.html:
A protocol lists operations a type promises to supply. A conformance is that type's implementation of the promise. Caption normally asks for a synchronous nonisolated caption. Row belongs to MainActor. The @MainActor before Caption in its conformance list restricts use of that implementation to MainActor, where caption can read its state. display is in the same domain. This syntax needs Swift 6.2 or newer; the earlier fixture run used 6.4. A new iOS deployment target alone cannot make an older compiler understand it.

protocol Caption { func caption() -> String }
@MainActor struct Row: @MainActor Caption {
    let name: String
    func caption() -> String { name }
}
@MainActor func display(_ row: Row) -> String { row.caption() }

Using this conformance on MainActor does not permit using it from every domain. For example, an @concurrent renderer requiring a nonisolated Caption and Sendable conformance cannot accept the isolated promise. The INVALID fixture checks that rejection. Making a @MainActor reference safe to pass does not give its protocol methods unrestricted access. A different design returns a Sendable CaptionSnapshot with a pure nonisolated implementation. That is an explicit model change. assumeIsolated asserts that execution is already in the required domain; it does not repair a caller that is in the wrong one.

The active OwnedViewModel declaration uses @MainActor DynamicProperty in its conformance list. That inspected source is a useful modern contract anchor, not evidence that all protocols in the client have been migrated. The analogous Android concern is satisfying a synchronous interface from UI-confined state. @UiThread documentation or dispatcher conventions do not give Java 11 the same isolated-conformance checking. Keep the comparison about requirements and callers rather than inventing equivalent annotations.

sections.title: Give older APIs one clear bridge owner
sections.html:
An adapter is a small boundary that turns one API's rules into another's. An older Objective-C or Swift API may omit Sendable annotations, call back on undocumented queues, or represent cancellation as another error. @preconcurrency import is a compatibility tool that can reduce certain imported Sendable diagnostics during an audit. It does not supply a lock, remove aliases or keep objects alive. Record which dependency needs it, what you assume about that dependency, who verifies those assumptions, and when the compatibility import can be removed.

Prefer constructing the legacy object inside its actor owner and returning Sendable results. If it truly requires a particular queue, wrapping it in an ordinary actor is not proof of that queue affinity. Document that requirement and use an appropriate adapter. If a callback hands over mutable data, copy the required fields before exposing them. A checked continuation is useful for one terminal result, but retain the existing exactly-once and cancellation tests rather than rebuilding their foundations here.

Define failures separately: transport failure remains an error, cancellation remains recognizable to the caller, and shutdown resolves pending work exactly once. A transfer does not automatically request cancellation or destroy the object. The receiving actor may retain it until an explicit reset. Cancelling the source task after installation is a request to stop that task; it does not give the source permission to use its transferred alias again. For uncertain cancellation-versus-installation schedules, select an acceptance point and use request identity to decide whether the receiver should commit. State ownership and operation acknowledgment are separate contracts.

quiz.question: What can sending permit for a non-Sendable class?
options: Unrestricted concurrent mutation by all aliases.
A checked transfer of a disconnected region across a boundary.
Automatic deep copying of every referenced child.
quiz.explanation: Sending permits a transfer when region rules are satisfied. It neither proves general sharing safety nor performs a deep copy; post-transfer aliases matter.

quiz.question: Why do Ledger calls inside batch need no await?
options: The isolated parameter puts the body in that ledger's domain.
All actors share MainActor.
Private setters disable suspension.
quiz.explanation: The concrete actor parameter selects isolation. The synchronous batch has no suspension; unrelated actors still have separate domains.

quiz.question: Does a MainActor-isolated Caption conformance satisfy every Sendable generic renderer?
options: Yes, because Sendable erases witness isolation.
Yes, after adding let.
No; the conformance's allowed use domain is independently checked.
quiz.explanation: Safely carrying a value or reference and freely invoking a conformance are different capabilities. The diagnostic fixture rejects the cross-domain conformance use.

exercise.brief: In your scratch copy, hand a mutable draft to one actor. Give an unrestricted renderer a separate read-only caption value.
steps: Run the valid and rejected transfer and conformance fixture cases.
Build an actor-owned handoff and make no source access through transferred aliases afterward.
Return a Sendable snapshot that both UI and renderer callers may use.
Name when the receiver accepts the draft and explain cancellation requests before and after that point.
acceptance: The fresh-draft transfer compiles, and the invalid use-after-transfer fixture is rejected.
The actor returns a String or Sendable struct instead of exposing its mutable draft.
The unrestricted renderer uses a value with a nonisolated protocol implementation.
The stop policy names an acceptance point and one owner responsible for cleanup.
exercise.solution:
Follow the DraftInbox pattern in Contracts.swift. Create a fresh Draft, pass it to install(_:) through sending, and observe it afterward only through the actor's snapshot(). If the sender must keep editing, first create a separate DraftSnapshot with text and revision. A wrapper that still holds the same mutable reference does not separate ownership, even if that wrapper's property is let. The INVALID fixture checks the forbidden source read after transfer. Such a read would leave the sender accessing state alongside its receiving actor.

struct CaptionSnapshot: Sendable, Caption {
    let name: String
    func caption() -> String { name }
}
// This declaration requires Caption from the section's complete protocol snippet.
// Keep Row's isolated conformance for UI callers; create a snapshot for other domains.

CaptionSnapshot supplies a pure protocol implementation from Sendable storage. If the module uses default MainActor inference, state the intended nonisolated type contract explicitly where needed and verify the consuming compiler settings. Passing a main-actor conformance through a generic function does not make it unrestricted. The conformance fixture checks both a valid same-domain use and a rejected concurrent generic use. The code above requires the Caption declaration from this lesson.

Choose installation as the acceptance point. Before that point, a sender that observes cancellation can stop and keep its local value. After the actor owns the value, cancelling the sender does not permit source mutation again. An account reset can clear actor state, or a generation check can reject an obsolete request under the service's stated policy. The transfer and isolated-batch host checks cover small language examples. Vendor callbacks, queue affinity, imported annotations and production cancellation require separate audits.

simple.story: Leena has a paper draft. She can give a sealed copy of its text to a colleague and keep editing her own paper. Or she can hand over the original and stop using it. If she keeps a second key to the drawer holding that original, the handoff is incomplete: two people could still edit the same sheet. After a complete handoff, the colleague keeps the paper in a controlled workspace and sends Leena a read-only report. Handing over that one sheet does not make every sheet in the workshop safe for everyone to edit.
simple.meaning: Sendable describes data safe across concurrency domains. sending requires a safe transfer at one boundary, with no conflicting source access to the transferred region. An actor can own the received mutable object and return Sendable snapshots. Actor isolation is an access rule, not a dedicated thread.

example.before: Inbox owns no draft. deliver creates a fresh Draft whose text is "fixture", with no other source use.
example.change: Await inbox.install(draft), whose parameter is sending Draft, then await inbox.snapshot().
example.after: Inbox owns the mutable draft and returns the String snapshot "fixture". The sender does not use the transferred reference again; Draft has not become a generally shareable type.

picture.caption: The Draft example transfers a mutable object and returns only its text.

items.label: Fresh Draft
items.text: deliver creates the disconnected mutable object with text "fixture".

items.label: sending boundary
items.text: install hands its isolation region to Inbox without later source access.

items.label: Actor-owned state
items.text: Inbox stores the draft under its isolation rules.

items.label: String snapshot
items.text: The caller receives "fixture", not the actor's mutable Draft reference.

words.meaning: A type contract for values that can cross concurrency domains safely under their access rules.
A parameter or result contract requiring a region safe to transfer across an isolation boundary.
Values and aliases the compiler tracks together when deciding whether a transfer is safe.
A separate view of selected state whose contents have a defined access and mutation policy.
An actor parameter that makes a function body execute within that actor's isolation.
A protocol implementation whose use is restricted to its declared actor domain.

simple.remember: A safe handoff is different from making a type safe to share.
simple.boundary: Swift checks reachable state and aliases, not paper or spare keys. sending does not deep-copy an object or mean consuming. Actor methods can interleave at suspension points, and transferred state can remain retained until the receiver explicitly clears it.

lessons.title: Clocks, task metadata and channels that wait for demand
lessons.summary: Test a deadline by advancing fake time, follow task-local metadata, and distinguish receiving a channel value from finishing its work.
objectives: Pass a Clock into timing code and check a deadline without guessing wall-clock delays.
Explain which tasks inherit task-local values and why that differs from lifetime and cancellation.
Explain why AsyncChannel receipt does not acknowledge completed processing.
Check how a zero-buffer channel removes cancelled waiters and finishes pending work.

sections.title: Give timing code a clock you can control
sections.html:
A stopwatch answers how much time passed. An appointment calendar answers which civil date to display. Swift's Clock is a dependency for elapsed timing: it provides a current Instant, a Duration type, and sleep until a deadline. An instant is a point on that clock's timeline; a duration is an amount to add to it. Android tests use virtual schedulers for a similar purpose. Pass the clock into the code being tested. Replacing one clock does not control unrelated Task.sleep calls, network callbacks or every scheduler.

Duration represents an elapsed amount with typed arithmetic rather than a naked integer of uncertain units. A deadline is an instant advanced by that amount. Neither is a calendar date. Use Foundation Date and Calendar for civil-time concerns such as appointment display, and use a monotonic clock for elapsed deadlines. ContinuousClock advances across system sleep; SuspendingClock pauses while the system is suspended. Suspending means system suspension, not an individual task awaiting a request.

Clock, Duration and these concrete clock types were introduced by Swift 5.7; Apple deployment availability for the concrete APIs must be checked for the target, commonly iOS 16/macOS 13. The companion's manual implementation additionally uses Synchronization on macOS 15. This is a host test requirement. A supported compiler can still reject a target API because its deployment minimum is too old. A wrapper needs either a compatible abstraction or an explicit availability-gated implementation.

sections.title: Register a deadline, then advance fake time
sections.html:
The function below computes a deadline from the clock it receives. C is a generic Clock type, and C.Duration ensures its delay belongs to that clock's duration type. using is the caller's argument label. A cancellation check asks whether a stop was requested before work starts. clock.now.advanced(by:) chooses the deadline. sleep can suspend the task and throw; it does not occupy a thread while waiting. nil tolerance leaves the implementation's default tolerance policy in effect. The final cancellation check protects the return of "ready" after wakeup. An already available deadline may complete without an actual suspension.

func delayed<C: Clock>(using clock: C, delay: C.Duration) async throws -> String {
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    let deadline = clock.now.advanced(by: delay)
    try await clock.sleep(until: deadline, tolerance: nil)
    try Task.checkCancellation()
    return "ready"
}

In the companion test, a task calls delayed with five virtual seconds. waitForSleeper establishes that registration happened. Advancing four seconds leaves one pending sleep; advancing the remaining second lets the task return ready. Another sleep is canceled after registration, joined as CancellationError, and removed. Advancing afterward must not resume that continuation again. These observations test deadline arithmetic and cleanup without depending on a millisecond wall-clock delay or Task.yield accidentally scheduling the desired task.

ManualClock's now requirement is synchronous, so its small storage helper uses a Mutex, releases it before resuming continuations, and never holds it across await. Its fake time starts at zero and moves only forward. It ignores tolerance because deterministic tests select exact deadlines; it is not a model of hardware scheduling jitter or a production clock. Clock injection makes a timing policy testable but does not prove timer punctuality, background execution allowance or real request latency.

sections.title: Carry request metadata with the task
sections.html:
A task-local value is metadata attached to task execution rather than to one thread. Here @TaskLocal declares an optional trace with default nil. The dollar-prefixed $trace exposes withValue, which binds "synthetic-trace" during a scope and restores the previous value afterward, including across suspension. async let creates a structured child that inherits it. Task creates unstructured work that also inherits task-local values at creation. Task.detached does not. The example awaits all three results, so it leaves none of these tasks independently running. Metadata inheritance alone does not give unstructured work a parent's lifetime or cancellation.

enum RequestContext {
    @TaskLocal static var trace: String?
}
func contextExample() async -> [String?] {
    await RequestContext.$trace.withValue("synthetic-trace") {
        async let child = readTrace()
        let inherited = Task { RequestContext.trace }
        let detached = Task.detached { RequestContext.trace }
        return await [child, inherited.value, detached.value]
    }
}
func readTrace() async -> String? { RequestContext.trace }

The expected array is synthetic-trace, synthetic-trace and nil. The companion additionally nests a different binding and verifies restoration, then verifies nil outside the original scope. An inherited binding in an unstructured task can outlive the lexical binding scope if its owner lets that task continue. Inheritance is therefore separate from structured lifetime and parent cancellation. Task-local storage is not a hidden cancellation token.

A Kotlin CoroutineContext element is a useful analogy for carrying request metadata through suspension; Java ThreadLocal alone does not follow work across thread changes. The exact inheritance APIs differ. TaskLocal's value should be Sendable immutable metadata, such as a synthetic trace label, not a globally shared mutable session object or real account secret. For independent detached work, capture a permitted value explicitly and bind it inside the new scope if that correlation is intentional.

sections.title: A waiting send controls demand, not processing completion
sections.html:
Backpressure means a producer waits for demand instead of freely sending more values. AsyncChannel provides a suspending send with that purpose. It belongs to Apple's open-source Swift AsyncAlgorithms package, which requires its own pinned dependency and tools/platform checks; importing Foundation does not supply it. The official guide describes a send waiting for an iterator to obtain its element. Obtaining is the acceptance being acknowledged. If a consumer then writes the element to a database, the send does not wait for that write to finish. A separate acknowledgment is needed for completed processing.

AsyncChannel.send is nonthrowing. Cancellation or finish can unblock it, so a returned send is not unconditional proof of delivery. Cancellation of one pending operation does not automatically cancel other tasks. Finish resumes pending operations and terminates iteration; a throwing channel additionally supports terminal failure. Follow the pinned API's behavior for termination and canceled iteration rather than translating it into a homegrown exception policy. Multiple producers and consumers do not make it a broadcast source or prove fairness.

Backpressure also does not guarantee a global memory bound if callers create an unbounded number of producer tasks, each retaining an element while awaiting send. Bound producers and payload sizes as well as buffered elements. AsyncStream bufferingNewest(1), already covered in session 017, instead drops older buffered values and does not suspend a callback producer. Kotlin Channel.RENDEZVOUS is a useful demand analogy, but Kotlin's canceled send exceptions and channel closing rules are not identical to AsyncChannel's nonthrowing send.

This lab deliberately has no remote package dependency. Its DemandChannel is a narrower teaching implementation with throwing send and next methods, zero accepted buffer, one pending sender and one pending receiver. It is not a reimplementation of every AsyncAlgorithms feature, an AsyncSequence conformance, or a production recommendation. The official package remains the reference for its own API.

sections.title: Choose one winner for receipt, cancellation or finish
sections.html:
A state machine names the allowed states and changes between them. DemandChannel begins open, with no accepted buffered value. If send finds a waiting receiver, it removes that receiver from state and resumes it with the element. If next finds a waiting sender, it removes that sender, returns its element and acknowledges receipt. Otherwise the operation stores one continuation, which is the means to resume it later. A second blocked sender or receiver is rejected as an overlapping call. Zero buffer therefore does not mean zero retained payloads: a pending sender holds its proposed value.

Each operation receives a unique serial identifier before its cancellation handler is installed. The handler schedules a short actor message to remove only the matching pending operation. Registration also checks Task.isCancelled to cover cancellation before that actor message arrives. Actor isolation keeps each match, cancel and finish decision separate from competing access; it does not give the channel a dedicated thread. Each decision takes the pending continuation out of state before resuming it. Removal is the terminal decision. A late cancellation message finds no matching continuation and does nothing.

A match accepts the delivery. If that decision wins before cancellation, a later stop request cannot take the element back. Processing may still observe cancellation and has its own commit rule. If cancellation wins first, a pending sender's proposed value is removed; a replacement can deliver. A cancelled receiver must not consume a future value. finish can be called repeatedly with the same effect. It rejects a pending sender with closed, resumes a pending receiver with nil, and prevents new sends. These are the local teaching rules. AsyncChannel.send has a different, nonthrowing termination contract.

The harness observation methods are event barriers, not production APIs. They must be used only when the test arranges the corresponding future registration. Calling waitForPendingSend after finish could wait forever. Keeping that limitation visible prevents a test helper from becoming an undocumented lifecycle abstraction.

sections.title: Finish and join work when a consumer leaves
sections.html:
Shutdown means deciding what happens to every operation still waiting. If a consumer leaves early, its owner must tell producers rather than just drop a reference. Dropping a task handle does not itself cancel or join that task. This lab explicitly calls finish and then joins stored task handles, meaning it awaits their terminal outcomes. A synchronous defer cannot await an actor's finish call. An asynchronous owner must arrange cleanup in both its ordinary and error paths. Otherwise an early consumer exit can leave a producer suspended indefinitely.

An upstream operation can throw while producing elements. Decide whether the owner records that error separately, adds a throwing terminal-result protocol, or uses AsyncThrowingChannel in a pinned package. DemandChannel.closed is a local shutdown condition, not evidence of successful upstream completion. Cancellation, ordinary failure and intentional end-of-input deserve different user-facing policies. A swallowed error followed by nil silently changes the contract.

If receipt is insufficient, send a command carrying a request identity and a separately owned acknowledgment mechanism, or use a request/response actor API. Bound outstanding acknowledgments and resolve them on consumer failure. Preserve generation checks for account or query changes after await. The new channel tests extend the existing course's continuation and stale-result tests by proving demand and registration cleanup; they do not replace business-level acceptance tests.

quiz.question: What does a channel send acknowledgment normally establish?
options: The consumer completed all later work.
The iterator accepted the element, subject to that API's termination/cancellation rules.
The element was broadcast to every subscriber.
quiz.explanation: Receipt and processing completion are separate contracts. AsyncChannel's nonthrowing send may also unblock on termination or cancellation; the local channel uses explicit errors.

quiz.question: Which task inherits the binding in contextExample?
options: Only detached.
Neither Task nor async let.
Both async let and Task, while detached sees the default.
quiz.explanation: Structured children and ordinary unstructured Task creation inherit task-local values. That does not give the unstructured task automatic parent cancellation or structured lifetime.

quiz.question: Why waitForSleeper before advancing fake time?
options: It establishes registration instead of guessing a scheduling delay.
It measures physical-device timer precision.
It converts the clock into Calendar.
quiz.explanation: The event barrier makes the interleaving deterministic. It provides no device timing evidence and uses elapsed-time instants, not civil dates.

exercise.brief: Check fake time, task metadata and channel waiting with a normal transfer, cancelled sender and receiver, and explicit shutdown.
steps: Predict all three task-context values and what nested binding restores.
Run the registered virtual-deadline and cancellation checks and keep their results.
Show that a cancelled pending sender can be replaced, then do the corresponding receiver case.
Explain receipt versus completed processing. On early exit, finish the channel and join its owned tasks.
acceptance: After advancing 4 of 5 seconds, one sleep remains pending; after the fifth second the joined result is ready.
A nested TaskLocal binding restores the outer value, while detached work sees nil.
Cancelled pending operations are removed, and their old values or receivers do not affect later transfers.
Finish resolves each pending operation once, and a new send after finish fails.
The report claims neither wall-clock punctuality nor runtime verification of AsyncAlgorithms.
exercise.solution:
First let a producer propose one integer. waitForPendingSend confirms it is registered. Calling next receives that integer; then join the producer. In the cancellation case, cancel the registered producer and join its CancellationError before offering a replacement value. The receiver should obtain only the replacement. Repeat from the receiver side: cancel and join the old waiter before sending to a new one. The two cases test different stored continuations, so passing one does not stand in for passing the other. A cancellation request must win the channel's state decision before it can remove that waiting operation.

For time, call delayed with ManualClock and a five-second delay. Await waitForSleeper before advancing four seconds. Inspect pendingSleeps, advance one more second, then join the task and check ready. Cancel a later registered sleep, verify its waiter was removed, and advance past its old deadline. The helper removes registrations before resuming, preventing that old continuation from being resumed twice. For context, bind the synthetic label, join the child and Task results, and join the detached task's nil result. Check restoration after the nested binding and after the outer scope too.

For shutdown, call await channel.finish(), then join the retained task. Test a blocked sender and a blocked receiver separately. Also check repeated finish and rejection of new sends. If matching already won, a later cancellation request cannot retract the receipt. Completing the received work requires a separate bounded acknowledgment; sender.value alone cannot establish that. The host package supplies the local teaching implementation. Native lifecycle cleanup and integration with a pinned AsyncAlgorithms version remain separate verification tasks.

simple.story: A kitchen practice game has a clock you move by hand. Nila sets a reminder for five seconds after zero. She first moves the clock to four. The reminder stays waiting because its deadline is five. She then moves it one more second and the reminder becomes ready. Nobody has to stand around for five real seconds. Before moving the clock, Nila checks that the reminder was actually registered. Otherwise she could advance time before the cook had even set it, and the game would test the wrong starting point.
simple.meaning: Injecting a Clock makes a timing rule controllable in a test. ManualClock starts at zero and advances only when instructed. The test waits for sleeper registration before advancing. This checks a deadline and cleanup, not physical timer precision or unrelated I/O.

example.before: A task calls delayed with ManualClock at 0 and delay 5 seconds. waitForSleeper confirms one registered sleep.
example.change: Advance the manual clock by 4 seconds, inspect pendingSleeps, then advance by 1 more second.
example.after: At 4 seconds there is still one pending sleep. At 5 seconds it can resume, and the joined task returns "ready" if cancellation has not been requested.

words.meaning: A source of instants with a defined way to sleep until a deadline.
A typed amount of elapsed time, separate from a calendar date.
Metadata bound to task execution that stays available through suspension, under its inheritance rules.
Making a producer wait for demand rather than freely admitting more work.
A sender and receiver meeting to transfer one value without an accepted buffer.
Confirmation that the consumer obtained a value, not that it completed the work caused by that value.
A stored way to resume an operation that is still waiting for a decision.

simple.boundary: ManualClock ignores real scheduling jitter and tolerance. Advancing it permits resumption but does not instantly run every task. It does not control networking or every sleep API. The local DemandChannel's throwing stop rules also differ from AsyncAlgorithms.

lessons.title: Owning, borrowing and releasing resources at the C boundary
lessons.summary: Track who owns native storage, which values are alive inside it, and which path releases it, including after errors or stop requests.
objectives: Tell object lifetime, exclusive mutation and cross-actor transfer apart.
Match initialized pointer storage and C resources with the right cleanup operations.
Account for Unmanaged's extra retain and keep temporary pointers inside their valid scope.
Check a small noncopyable owner's borrowed reads and one consuming extraction.

sections.title: Ask who owns the resource and who releases it
sections.html:
Owning a resource means being responsible for keeping it valid and eventually releasing it. Borrowing means using it for a limited time under the owner's rules. An Android JNI call already makes you distinguish managed objects from native buffers and handles. Swift has separate rules too: ARC manages strong class references, exclusivity prevents conflicting storage access, and Sendable or sending governs concurrency boundaries. None of these alone proves an arbitrary C pointer remains valid. Before choosing syntax, name each owner, each permitted borrower and the event that ends access.

Sessions 004 and 039 cover retain cycles, copy-on-write and allocation evidence; session 064 covers basic inout exclusivity. This lesson extends those foundations with a compiler-negative exclusivity fixture, scoped allocation, a small Unmanaged retain balance and a noncopyable owner. It is a bounded elective. It does not teach every foreign ABI, Core Foundation ownership exception, or unsafe performance technique. Those require their own documentation and specialist review.

Do not adopt unsafe storage merely because a struct is copied or ARC appears in a profile. Establish a measured problem first. The examples here use synthetic integers and release all owned storage within a known scope. No dangling-pointer, double-free or data-race demonstration is executed. Rejected programs stay compiler fixtures, so a learning failure does not become an unsafe host run.

sections.title: One writable access must not conflict with another
sections.html:
Exclusivity is a rule about overlapping access, even on one thread. inout gives a parameter writable access for the duration of a call. At the call site, the ampersand marks that access; it does not permit storing a pointer for later. exchange saves the first value, writes the second into the first, and writes the saved value into the second. Two distinct variables starting at 1 and 2 therefore return (2, 1). The diagnostic alternative passes first twice, creating two overlapping writable accesses to the same storage. The companion compiles that invalid fixture only and records its rejection.

func exchange(_ first: inout Int, _ second: inout Int) {
    let saved = first
    first = second
    second = saved
}
func valid() -> (Int, Int) {
    var first = 1
    var second = 2
    exchange(&first, &second)
    return (first, second)
}
// Diagnostic-only alternative: exchange(&first, &first)

This rule is independent of multithreading. A program can violate exclusivity through a nested read while one mutation remains active. Some conflicts are diagnosed statically, and others require runtime enforcement. A passing compile is therefore not a proof that every dynamically selected access is disjoint. For array element exchanges, prefer the collection's swapAt operation rather than constructing potentially overlapping inout subscripts.

Java references and Kotlin mutable receivers lack this exact language access model. Their ability to alias two parameters does not predict Swift's behavior. Unsafe pointers can bypass some checked accesses, but that moves the proof obligation to the author. Borrowing a value, mutating it through inout, and consuming its ownership are different operations. They cannot be freely overlapped just because the code remains on one actor.

sections.title: Reserve storage, start values, then clean up both
sections.html:
Storage and the live values inside it are different things. allocate(capacity: 2) reserves room for two Int values without initializing them. initialize(repeating: 4, count: 2) starts both values' lifetimes. Reading them now yields 4 + 4, or 8. The defer registers cleanup: deinitialize ends those two lifetimes, and deallocate releases the storage. The returned Int is independent of the pointer. Replacing an already initialized value would use assignment instead of initialization. In a throwing variant, a later error after this defer registration would take the same cleanup path. The companion checks this bounded function's result.

func scopedSum() -> Int {
    let pointer = UnsafeMutablePointer<Int>.allocate(capacity: 2)
    pointer.initialize(repeating: 4, count: 2)
    defer {
        pointer.deinitialize(count: 2)
        pointer.deallocate()
    }
    return pointer[0] + pointer[1]
}

With nontrivial element types, skipping deinitialization can leak their retained objects. Deinitializing uninitialized slots or reading beyond capacity is invalid. If initialization can partially succeed, track the initialized count and destroy only those elements. If allocation belongs to a C API, use its documented destructor rather than Swift's deallocate. Matching allocator families matters: storage from malloc belongs to free, and getifaddrs results belong to freeifaddrs. A Swift typed allocation is not interchangeable with either.

MemoryLayout.size counts a value's size, stride gives spacing between consecutive values, and alignment restricts valid starting addresses. Typed allocation handles its element alignment. Raw storage and type binding still need correct type, count and lifetime rules. Do not turn arbitrary bytes into a class object, or assume a network packet matches a Swift struct's memory layout. Check the C function's status and output length before constructing Swift values. An empty buffer can validly have a nil base address; a count of zero does not promise an address you can dereference.

sections.title: Use a temporary pointer only while its closure runs
sections.html:
A borrowed pointer is permission to access storage for the window an API promises. withUnsafeBufferPointer exposes an array's contiguous storage only during its closure. The array still owns that storage; buffer is a temporary view. byteCount returns buffer.count, an ordinary integer, so it exposes no address for later use. An empty array is safe here because the body needs only its count; an empty buffer can have a nil base address. This standalone function needs no Foundation import. Storing baseAddress for a later callback would break the API's validity promise.

func byteCount(_ values: [UInt8]) -> Int {
    values.withUnsafeBufferPointer { buffer in
        // Read only inside this closure; never store buffer.baseAddress.
        buffer.count
    }
}

The same constraint applies to withUnsafePointer(to:) and Data.withUnsafeBytes: their closure delimits the promised validity. If a C function stores the pointer after it returns, a temporary Swift borrow is the wrong adapter. Use stable owned storage with an explicit release path, or choose an API that copies the input. Do not suspend or move a borrowed pointer into an independent task and assume ARC pins the bytes. A retained Array binding alone does not establish all representation and mutation guarantees for an escaped temporary pointer.

The inspected client Data extension reads an IPv4 buffer within withUnsafeBytes and returns a String; its IPv6 branch also allocates output C characters and deallocates them after constructing a String. These are concrete boundaries to trace, not runtime evidence of every status or input path. The separate UIDevice extension obtains a C interface list and later calls freeifaddrs. Client source stays unchanged. A future audit should check all C status returns, lengths, early exits and ownership annotations, independently from this host exercise.

sections.title: Count each extra object retain and hand it back once
sections.html:
A retain is an ownership obligation that keeps an object alive. Unmanaged exposes such obligations when crossing APIs that carry raw context pointers. passRetained(box) creates one extra strong reference, called +1. toOpaque changes it to a raw context token without balancing that retain. fromOpaque reconstructs the correctly typed view. takeRetainedValue hands the outstanding +1 back into a managed Swift reference, recovered. Its normal ARC lifetime then keeps the object valid while recovered.value is read and releases that ownership when it ends. This pair balances one path; it does not manage callback timing or make a pointer safe to share.

final class CallbackBox {
    let value: Int
    init(_ value: Int) { self.value = value }
}
func retainedRoundTrip(_ box: CallbackBox) -> Int {
    let context = Unmanaged.passRetained(box).toOpaque()
    let recovered = Unmanaged<CallbackBox>.fromOpaque(context).takeRetainedValue()
    return recovered.value
}

This function simulates a synchronous C API returning one owned context exactly once. It is not an asynchronous callback adapter. The companion holds only a weak observation after the caller's scope and confirms the box is released; that detects an extra retain left by this particular path. It does not prove that an unrelated vendor callback fires exactly once.

PassUnretained provides no extra lifetime. TakeUnretainedValue does not balance an owned +1. Those operations are appropriate only when another documented owner keeps the object alive for the access. For a repeating callback, the registration may own one retained context until unregister and callback quiescence, meaning no callback can still access it. Each callback should borrow the context rather than consume its only retain. For a one-shot callback, completion and cancellation must agree on which path consumes or releases the +1. If C can call back after cancellation, releasing immediately can leave it with an invalid pointer. Capture shutdown acknowledgment and ownership rather than guessing from a canceled Swift task.

sections.title: Borrow to read; consume to end this owner's use
sections.html:
A noncopyable type cannot freely duplicate its owned value. ~Copyable removes the usual Copyable requirement; the tilde here is not bitwise negation. OwnedInt keeps one allocation private, initializes its integer, and releases it in deinit. borrowing read accesses the value without consuming the owner. consuming extract takes ownership of self and returns an independent Int. When that consumed owner is destroyed, deinit ends the stored value and releases the allocation. A caller cannot then read the same consumed binding again. The compiler rejects that reuse; it does not inspect every unsafe pointer operation for correctness.

struct OwnedInt: ~Copyable {
    private let storage: UnsafeMutablePointer<Int>
    init(_ value: Int) {
        storage = .allocate(capacity: 1)
        storage.initialize(to: value)
    }
    borrowing func read() -> Int { storage.pointee }
    consuming func extract() -> Int { storage.pointee }
    deinit {
        storage.deinitialize(count: 1)
        storage.deallocate()
    }
}

Swift 5.9 introduced noncopyable structs/enums and explicit borrowing/consuming modifiers. Later compilers expanded their generic and protocol support; the course package requires 6.2 rather than promising every modern pattern on 5.9. Ordinary generics traditionally assume Copyable; lifting that constraint with ~Copyable is an additional capability to learn deliberately. This example stays within a small concrete type and runs under the local Swift 6.4 toolchain.

Noncopyable is not Sendable, and a unique owner does not automatically make its unsafe pointer safe to access from another executor. It also does not verify the implementation of deinit or every C call. A Java AutoCloseable or Kotlin use block offers scope cleanup but generally permits aliasing or calling close twice. Swift's consumed-value rule prevents some duplicate-owner programs at compilation. That difference is useful, but neither makes all native code safe by construction.

sections.title: A stop request does not release storage immediately
sections.html:
A cancellation request sets a task's stop flag; it does not reach in and free its resources. Cleanup happens when the relevant owner exits or is destroyed. When practical, check for the request before allocating. Then keep the resource under one scoped owner if later work can throw. deinit and defer can perform synchronous memory cleanup, but they cannot await a foreign API's shutdown acknowledgment. If that API may still call back, explicitly stop it and obtain confirmation that callbacks have ceased before finally releasing the context they use.

In a review, list allocation source, initialized count, retained context count, borrower scopes, callback repetition, accepted cancellation and final release. Require exactly one owner for each terminal path and no return of borrowed addresses. The host checks values and one weak lifetime observation, while compiler fixtures verify consumed-value and aliasing rejection. Sanitizer runs, native callback stress schedules, C ABI auditing and production memory traces remain further practice. Do not convert those pending checks into claimed evidence just because the small package passes.

quiz.question: Which cleanup pairs with initialized Swift typed allocation?
options: free regardless of allocator.
Deinitialize the initialized elements, then deallocate.
takeUnretainedValue on the pointer.
quiz.explanation: Typed storage and element lifetimes require matching operations. C allocators have their own destructors; Unmanaged applies to object references, not raw typed allocations.

quiz.question: What does passRetained followed by takeRetainedValue establish?
options: An owned +1 is handed back to managed Swift ownership.
The callback can repeat without limit.
The raw pointer became Sendable.
quiz.explanation: The pair balances one retain obligation on this path. Callback cardinality, cancellation quiescence and cross-domain safety need independent contracts.

quiz.question: Why cannot read follow extract on the same noncopyable owner?
options: Int values cannot be read twice.
Every read deallocates storage.
extract consumes self, ending the caller's ownership.
quiz.explanation: Borrowing read preserves the owner; consuming extract transfers its ownership and the consumed binding cannot be reused. The compiler rejects that fixture.

exercise.brief: Explain who owns each resource in a typed allocation, an object context and a noncopyable owner. Check their valid results and rejected misuse cases.
steps: Run the ownership and exclusivity compiler cases without executing the invalid branches.
In Contracts.swift, explain each operation that reserves storage, starts a value, ends a value or releases ownership.
Check that borrowed reads occur before consumption and that extraction consumes the owner once.
Describe how a repeating C callback stops and confirms no callback can still use its context before release.
acceptance: The scoped allocation returns 8 and exposes no address.
OwnedInt reads and extracts 42; the reuse-after-consumption fixture is rejected.
The synchronous retained context returns its value, and the weak observation becomes nil after the owner's scope.
Callback notes distinguish temporary access from registration ownership and require callbacks to cease before final release.
The report states which compiler and host checks ran, with native ABI and sanitizer checks still pending.
exercise.solution:
Start by counting storage and live values separately. scopedSum reserves two uninitialized slots, initializes each to 4, registers defer, and reads the sum 8. Cleanup ends exactly two value lifetimes, then uses deallocate because Swift's typed allocator supplied the storage. In a throwing version, an error after cleanup registration follows that same path. If initialization succeeds for only some elements, track that initialized count and destroy only those elements; blindly deinitializing the entire capacity would be invalid.

Create OwnedInt(42). Use borrowing read once or several times, then consuming extract once. The returned Int can outlive the destroyed allocation because it contains the value, not an address. Diagnostics/Ownership.swift compiles the valid path and rejects reuse in its INVALID branch. This verifies the exposed use boundary and the sample result, not every possible unsafe implementation. Exclusivity.swift separately rejects two simultaneous inout accesses to one local variable.

Balance one passRetained with one takeRetainedValue in the synchronous context round trip. The weak observation checks whether that path leaked an extra retain. For repeated callbacks, keep one retain owned by the registration and borrow it in each callback. Stop registration, obtain a guarantee that no callback can still access the context, then release once. A Swift task's cancellation request does not supply that guarantee unless the foreign API documents it. Native callback adapters, platform status paths and sanitizer checks still need separate work. Use this answer as a reference while making your own predictions and collecting evidence.

simple.story: A baker reserves space for two trays before putting food on them. Empty reserved space is not yet a meal. She puts four crackers on each tray, counts eight, and writes that number on a receipt. Before giving back the reserved space, she removes the crackers from both trays. The receipt can leave the bakery because it contains a number, not the trays themselves. If another worker only borrows a tray to count it, the worker must finish before the baker removes its contents and releases the space.
simple.meaning: Allocation reserves storage; initialization starts the values' lifetimes. Reads must stay within initialized storage. Deinitialization ends those lifetimes, then deallocation releases the allocation. A returned Int can outlive the storage. Borrowed pointers have a limited validity window, not independent ownership.

example.before: scopedSum allocates capacity for 2 Int values. Both slots are initially uninitialized and must not be read.
example.change: Initialize both slots to 4, register defer cleanup, and compute pointer[0] + pointer[1].
example.after: The function returns 8. defer deinitializes 2 values and deallocates their storage. The returned Int contains no borrowed address.

words.meaning: Swift's rule preventing conflicting accesses while one writable access to storage is active.
Reserving a region of storage with a size, alignment and matching release operation.
Beginning a value's lifetime in storage; it differs from replacing an already live value.
An address usable only during the validity window its owning API promises.
A wrapper exposing explicit object-retain obligations without automatically balancing them for you.
Borrowing accesses an owner without taking it; consuming transfers that ownership and prevents reuse of the consumed binding.
A type whose owned value cannot be freely copied to create another independent owner.

simple.remember: Know the owner, the valid access window and the matching release.
simple.boundary: Memory contains typed values, not crackers. Unsafe pointers can bypass checks, and noncopyability does not prove a pointer implementation safe or Sendable. C allocators need their own matching destructors, and a cancellation request does not immediately free resources.
